There are few things that parents care more about than the education of their children. For teachers and headteachers, it is stressful and exposing to have their work judged. At a time when shrinking school rolls are leading to closures, the stakes are even higher. An unpopular school with empty places is far more likely to be asked to merge, or close, than one that is sought after by parents. Policymakers have a tough job to strike a balance between the undeniable pressure that the watchdog places on schools in England and the benefits to families of information to aid their choices. But the coroner’s verdict on the death of Ruth Perry, a headteacher who took her own life in 2023, tipped the balance away from a system that relied too heavily on one-word judgments . stories.description: Ten years after full extent of problem was revealed, Guardian investigation finds schools facing uphill battle amid rapid societal changes Thousands of child-on-child sexual offences reported at schools in England and Wales It is 10 years since a report first revealed the epic scale of sexual bullying, harassment and abuse girls faced in England’s schools on a daily basis. The report , by MPs on the women and equalities committee, showed the horrifying normality of child-on-child abuse in schools. The need for government action was “overwhelming”, said the committee chair, Maria Miller. Ofsted duly investigated, recommendations were written, promises were made and a new sex education curriculum was rolled out. Continue reading...

stories.title: ‘Just like my big brothers’: boy with cerebral palsy passes GCSEs with eye-tracking technology
stories.description: Patrick McCabe’s herculean feat shows limits and possibilities of special educational needs and disabilities system Patrick McCabe is instantly recognisable in the early autumn sunshine, his wheelchair surrounded by fellow pupils at Fallibroome Academy in Macclesfield, Cheshire as they move from lesson to lesson, chatting, laughing and joking around. His extraordinary GCSE success this summer has become the stuff of legend. The 16-year-old has cerebral palsy and it took four months for him to complete his exams using eye-tracking technology. Now Patrick has started his A-levels – French, business and media studies – and fresh challenges lie ahead. Continue reading...
